blocks.body:
A poll of 400 voters finds that 58% support a new park. Nobody believes the true figure for the whole town is exactly 58%: a different 400 voters would have given a slightly different answer. The useful question is how far off the 58% might plausibly be. A confidence interval answers it with a range such as "between 53% and 63%", together with a precise statement of how much trust the method deserves.

To build one we need to know how a sample statistic behaves when the sampling is repeated. That behaviour, the sampling distribution, rests on random sampling ([[sampling-design]]), which makes the variation predictable, and on the central limit theorem ([[limit-theorems]]), which gives its shape.

blocks.title: A statistic is a random quantity
blocks.body:
A parameter is a number describing the whole population, such as the true proportion $p$ of supporters. A statistic is a number computed from a random sample of size $n$, such as the sample proportion $\hat p$ (read "p-hat"). If we could repeat the sampling many times, $\hat p$ would take many values. The distribution of those values is the sampling distribution of $\hat p$.

A tiny example makes this concrete. Suppose $p = 0.4$ and we sample $n = 5$ people independently. The number of supporters $K$ is binomial, and $\hat p = K/5$ has this distribution:

- $\hat p = 0$: probability $0.07776$
- $\hat p = 0.2$: probability $0.2592$
- $\hat p = 0.4$: probability $0.3456$
- $\hat p = 0.6$: probability $0.2304$
- $\hat p = 0.8$: probability $0.0768$
- $\hat p = 1$: probability $0.01024$

The values are centred at $0.4$, the true $p$, but the spread is large: with only 5 people, a sample showing $0.8$ or more happens almost 9% of the time. With larger $n$ the same picture becomes narrower and more bell-shaped.

blocks.title: Mean and spread of the sample proportion and the sample mean
blocks.body:
Let $X_1,\dots,X_n$ be independent, each with mean $\mu$ and standard deviation $\sigma$, and let $\bar X = \frac1n(X_1+\dots+X_n)$. Then
$$\operatorname{E}[\bar X] = \mu, \qquad \operatorname{SD}(\bar X) = \frac{\sigma}{\sqrt n}.$$
In particular, if each $X_i$ is $1$ (success) with probability $p$ and $0$ otherwise, then $\bar X = \hat p$ and
$$\operatorname{E}[\hat p] = p, \qquad \operatorname{SD}(\hat p) = \sqrt{\frac{p(1-p)}{n}}.$$

Expectation is linear, so $\operatorname{E}[\bar X] = \frac1n(\mu+\dots+\mu) = \mu$. Variances of independent variables add, and $\operatorname{Var}(cY) = c^2\operatorname{Var}(Y)$, so
$$\operatorname{Var}(\bar X) = \frac{1}{n^2}\big(\operatorname{Var}(X_1)+\dots+\operatorname{Var}(X_n)\big) = \frac{n\sigma^2}{n^2} = \frac{\sigma^2}{n}.$$
Taking square roots gives $\sigma/\sqrt n$. For a $0/1$ variable, $\operatorname{E}[X_i] = p$ and $\operatorname{E}[X_i^2] = p$, so $\operatorname{Var}(X_i) = p - p^2 = p(1-p)$; substitute this for $\sigma^2$.

blocks.title: Shape: the central limit theorem
blocks.body:
The theorem gives the centre and spread; the central limit theorem gives the shape. For large $n$ the sampling distribution of $\bar X$ is approximately normal, whatever the shape of the population, so
$$Z = \frac{\bar X - \mu}{\sigma/\sqrt n}$$
is approximately standard normal. For a proportion the usual rule of thumb is that the approximation is reasonable when $np \ge 10$ and $n(1-p) \ge 10$ (some textbooks use 5). If the population itself is normal, $\bar X$ is exactly normal for every $n$.

The standard deviation of a statistic has its own name, the standard error, especially when unknown parameters in it are replaced by estimates. For a proportion the standard error is $\sqrt{\hat p(1-\hat p)/n}$.

These formulas assume independent observations. When sampling without replacement from a finite population, the observations are nearly independent if the sample is at most about 10% of the population. The $\sqrt n$ is the key feature: to halve the standard error you need four times as many observations.

blocks.title: From sampling distribution to interval
blocks.body:
For a standard normal $Z$, $P(-1.96 \le Z \le 1.96) \approx 0.95$. Applying this to the standardised $\bar X$,
$$P\Big(-1.96 \le \frac{\bar X-\mu}{\sigma/\sqrt n} \le 1.96\Big) \approx 0.95.$$
Rearranging the inequalities to isolate $\mu$ gives
$$P\Big(\bar X - 1.96\tfrac{\sigma}{\sqrt n} \le \mu \le \bar X + 1.96\tfrac{\sigma}{\sqrt n}\Big) \approx 0.95.$$
The endpoints are random (they depend on the sample) and $\mu$ is fixed. So the random interval $\bar X \pm 1.96\,\sigma/\sqrt n$ contains $\mu$ with probability about $0.95$.

Other confidence levels use other critical values $z^*$, where $P(-z^* \le Z \le z^*)$ equals the level: $z^* \approx 1.645$ for 90%, $1.960$ for 95% and $2.576$ for 99%. Higher confidence means a wider interval. The quantity $z^*\cdot\text{SE}$ is the margin of error.

blocks.title: Confidence interval
blocks.body:
A level $C$ confidence interval for a parameter $\theta$ is a pair of statistics $L \le U$, computed from the sample, such that
$$P(L \le \theta \le U) = C$$
for every possible value of $\theta$ (exactly, or approximately for large samples). The standard large-sample intervals are
$$\hat p \pm z^*\sqrt{\frac{\hat p(1-\hat p)}{n}} \quad\text{for a proportion}, \qquad \bar x \pm z^*\frac{\sigma}{\sqrt n} \quad\text{for a mean with known } \sigma.$$

The probability describes the method, before the data are seen, not a particular interval after the data are seen.

blocks.title: What 95% confidence does and does not mean
blocks.body:
Once the poll gives $(0.532, 0.628)$, the true $p$ is either inside it or not; there is nothing random left. The correct reading is: "this interval was produced by a method that captures the true value in 95% of samples." If 100 pollsters each took their own random sample, about 95 of their intervals would contain $p$, and no pollster could tell from her own data whether hers is one of the misses.

The statement "there is a 95% probability that $p$ lies in $(0.532, 0.628)$" treats $p$ as random. That is the language of Bayesian statistics, which requires a prior distribution for $p$, and it is not what a confidence interval asserts.

Also notice what the margin of error leaves out. It accounts only for random sampling variation. A badly worded question, a sample of volunteers or people refusing to answer can bias the result far more than the margin of error suggests; see [[sampling-design]].

blocks.title: A poll
blocks.body: In a made-up poll, 232 of 400 randomly chosen voters support the park. Give a 95% confidence interval for the proportion of all voters who support it, and check the conditions.
blocks.solution:
Here $\hat p = 232/400 = 0.58$. The successes and failures, 232 and 168, are both at least 10, and 400 is a small fraction of a town's voters, so the normal approximation is reasonable. The standard error is
$$\text{SE} = \sqrt{\frac{0.58 \times 0.42}{400}} \approx 0.02468,$$
so the margin of error is $1.96 \times 0.02468 \approx 0.0484$ and the interval is
$$0.58 \pm 0.048 = (0.532,\ 0.628).$$
We are 95% confident that between about 53% and 63% of voters support the park. Since the whole interval lies above 50%, the data are evidence of majority support, an idea made precise in [[hypothesis-testing]].

blocks.title: A mean with known standard deviation
blocks.body:
Heights of adult women in a region are known to be normally distributed with standard deviation $6$ cm. A made-up random sample of 8 heights (cm) is
$$162,\ 170,\ 158,\ 175,\ 168,\ 166,\ 171,\ 160.$$
Find a 95% confidence interval for the mean height.
blocks.solution:
The sum is $1330$, so $\bar x = 166.25$. Because the population is normal, $\bar X$ is exactly normal even though $n = 8$ is small, and the interval is
$$166.25 \pm 1.96\cdot\frac{6}{\sqrt 8} = 166.25 \pm 4.16 = (162.09,\ 170.41).$$
In practice $\sigma$ is rarely known. If we estimate it by the sample standard deviation, the critical value $1.96$ must be replaced by a larger one from the $t$-distribution; see [[t-tests]].

blocks.title: How large a sample?
blocks.body: A newspaper wants a 95% margin of error of at most 3 percentage points for a proportion, without any idea what the proportion is. How many people must it sample?
blocks.solution:
We need $1.96\sqrt{p(1-p)/n} \le 0.03$. The product $p(1-p)$ is largest at $p = 1/2$, where it equals $1/4$, because $p(1-p) = \tfrac14 - (p-\tfrac12)^2$. So it is enough that
$$1.96\cdot\frac{1}{2\sqrt n} \le 0.03 \iff n \ge \Big(\frac{1.96}{0.06}\Big)^2 \approx 1067.1.$$
A sample of $1068$ guarantees the target whatever $p$ is. This is why so many national polls have about a thousand respondents, whatever the size of the country: the margin depends on $n$, not on the population size.

blocks.title: Comparing two groups
blocks.body: In a made-up experiment, 45 of 150 people shown advert A and 30 of 150 shown advert B bought the product. Give a 95% confidence interval for the difference $p_A - p_B$ of the purchase rates.
blocks.solution:
Conditions: the people were randomly assigned to two separate groups, and each group has at least 10 buyers and 10 non-buyers (45 and 105, 30 and 120). The two groups are independent, so the variance of $\hat p_A - \hat p_B$ is the sum of the two variances, and
$$\text{SE} = \sqrt{\frac{0.30\times 0.70}{150} + \frac{0.20\times 0.80}{150}} \approx 0.0497.$$
The interval is $0.10 \pm 1.96\times 0.0497 = 0.10 \pm 0.097 = (0.003,\ 0.197)$. It lies just above zero, so the data favour advert A, but the size of the advantage is very uncertain: anything from almost nothing to about 20 points is plausible.

blocks.title: When nothing happens: the rule of three
blocks.body: A new process produces $n$ items and none is faulty. The interval $\hat p \pm 1.96\sqrt{\hat p(1-\hat p)/n}$ collapses to the single point $0$, which is clearly too optimistic. Instead, take as plausible all values of $p$ under which seeing no faults has probability at least $0.05$. Show that this set is $[0, p_0]$ with $p_0 = 1 - 0.05^{1/n}$, and that $p_0 < 3/n$.
blocks.solution:
The probability of no faults is $(1-p)^n$, which decreases as $p$ increases. So $(1-p)^n \ge 0.05$ exactly when $1 - p \ge 0.05^{1/n}$, that is $p \le p_0 = 1 - 0.05^{1/n}$.

Write $0.05^{1/n} = e^{-(\ln 20)/n}$. For every $x > 0$ we have $e^{-x} > 1 - x$ (the curve $e^{-x}$ lies above its tangent line at $0$). With $x = (\ln 20)/n$ this gives
$$p_0 = 1 - e^{-(\ln 20)/n} < \frac{\ln 20}{n} < \frac{3}{n},$$
since $\ln 20 \approx 2.996$. For $n = 100$, $p_0 \approx 0.0295$. So after 100 fault-free items we can still only say the fault rate is probably below about 3%. This kind of interval, obtained by collecting the parameter values the data do not reject, is the bridge to [[hypothesis-testing]].

blocks.title: Going further: exact coverage and better intervals
blocks.body:
The proportion interval $\hat p \pm z^*\sqrt{\hat p(1-\hat p)/n}$ is called the Wald interval. Its true coverage can be computed exactly by adding binomial probabilities over all outcomes $k$ whose interval contains $p$. For $n = 400$ and $p = 0.58$ the coverage is about $0.946$, close to the nominal $0.95$. For $n = 20$ and $p = 0.1$ it is only about $0.876$: when $np$ is small the normal approximation fails; for instance $\hat p = 0$, which happens with probability $0.9^{20} \approx 0.12$, gives an interval of zero width.

A better method inverts the approximate test directly: keep every $p$ with $|\hat p - p| \le z^*\sqrt{p(1-p)/n}$, using the true $p$ in the standard error rather than $\hat p$. Solving this quadratic inequality in $p$ gives the Wilson interval, which never collapses to a point and has coverage much closer to the nominal level (see Agresti and Coull). For the poll it gives $(0.531, 0.627)$, almost the same as before; the two differ a lot only when $n$ is small or $\hat p$ is near $0$ or $1$.

The general recipe is a pivot: a function of data and parameter, like $(\bar X-\mu)/(\sigma/\sqrt n)$, whose distribution does not depend on the parameter; inverting probability statements about it yields intervals. Intervals and tests are two views of one object: a 95% interval consists of exactly the parameter values that a 5%-level test would not reject. For a systematic theory of the estimators themselves, see [[point-estimation]].

- A 95% interval does not contain 95% of the data, and it does not say that a new observation will fall inside it. It is about the parameter.
- The normal approximation for proportions needs enough successes and failures; with few of either, use an exact or Wilson interval.
- For a difference of two independent groups, the standard errors do not add; their squares (the variances) do.

Confidence intervals and [[hypothesis-testing]] are built from the same sampling distributions. When $\sigma$ must be estimated, the normal critical values give way to the $t$-distribution of [[t-tests]]. The estimators placed at the centre of an interval, and the reason $\hat p$ and $\bar x$ are good choices, are studied in [[point-estimation]]. The same $\sigma/\sqrt n$ error bar controls the accuracy of [[monte-carlo]] simulation.

1. A made-up survey finds that 90 of 250 students walk to school. Compute a 90% confidence interval for the proportion of all students who walk.
2. A 95% interval for a mean is $(48.2, 51.8)$, computed from a sample of 36 with known $\sigma$. What were $\bar x$ and $\sigma$?
3. How large must $n$ be for a 99% margin of error of at most 2 percentage points, with no prior knowledge of $p$?

sources.ref: Agresti & Coull, Approximate is better than 'exact' for interval estimation of binomial proportions, The American Statistician (1998)
